Lessons.Title: Use Factors to Find Equivalent Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: First Edition 2021 Grade4 Unit2 Lesson11: inverse numerical strategy for generating equivalent fractions. Divide BOTH numerator and denominator by same common whole-number factor; previous lesson multiplied both. Source original 5-page Student Task Statements and local teacher narrative reviewed.

Warm-up Which One Doesn't Belong (10min): teacher displays four original fraction illustrations A–D, with one of them the written1/4. Partner describes visual/equivalence argument, not a single automatically graded response. Images belong to source, no unverified replacement claimed.

Activity1 The Other Way Around (20min): Andre represents8/12 using a number line and dark grouping marks; Kiran's matching divisions8÷4 over12÷4=2/3 and8÷2 over12÷2=4/6. Discuss each matching point. Independent source targets:10/12=5/6;18/12=9/6=6/4=3/2 using nontrivial common divisors2,3,6. These equivalent fractions describe the same distance from0.

Activity2 How Would You Find Them (15min): original FIVE targets16/8,40/10,7/6,90/100,5/4. Learners supply at least TWO different equivalent fractions for EACH target. They may divide when both numbers have common factors, multiply otherwise; eg7/6 and5/4 require multiplication for a new integer numerator/denominator. Mathematical explanations teacher-reviewed.

Activity3 OPTIONAL Card Sort: Fractions Galore (15min): group3–4 students with36 original teacher-supplied fraction cards from 2021 5-page blackline source. Find as many equivalent groups as possible, record unmatched fractions and defend reasoning. This is optional, not 36 mandatory digital questions; source Blackline text/images not represented as copied app art.
Student Section Summary: equivalent fractions occupy same location on number lines, multiplication and common-factor division produce equivalent numerator/denominator names.

Independent first-party Edulytics five-minute Cool-down, NOT source publisher protected original: show two ways of reducing8/12 to2/3 and4/6, and two equivalents of5/4. Teacher assesses the reasoning; existing exact reduction/equivalence skills are numeric supplements.

KeyConcepts.Title: Common-factor reduction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Divide numerator and denominator by a positive whole-number divisor common to both.
KeyConcepts.Rule: (a÷n)/(b÷n)=a/b if n divides a,b and b,n>0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent using multiplication
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply numerator and denominator by the same positive factor.

KeyConcepts.Title: Method choice
KeyConcepts.Definition: Large reducible fractions can be divided; irreducible ones can be multiplied for new examples.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Never divide by a number not a common whole-number factor.

WorkedExamples.Title: Andre/Kiran's source twelfths
WorkedExamples.Question: Give two fractions equivalent to8/12.
Steps: All locate same point on matching number lines.

WorkedExamples.Question: How can7/6 have two different equivalents?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dividing only numerator or by unrelated divisors.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: This changes fraction value or gives non-whole parts.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use one common positive integer factor for both.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming the optional blackline 36-card sort is auto-graded.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source is a physical student group activity with flexible groupings.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher supplies the original cards and assesses peer evidence.
